claims.source: Together these results demonstrate that loss of either cardiac hepcidin or hepcidin responsiveness in the heart results in upregulation of cardiomyocyte FPN, and that cardiomyocytes of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts are iron deficient as a result of upregulation of FPN-mediated iron export.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of increased Fe55 efflux, decreased cardiomyocyte iron content, and upregulation of iron deficiency markers in both mouse models.

claims.claim: The LV enlargement and the reduced LVEF, seen in untreated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, were prevented in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
claims.source: At this timepoint, we performed cine MRI and found that the LV enlargement and the reduced LVEF, seen in untreated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, were prevented in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice (Figure 4A–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by cine MRI measurements of LVES, LVED, and LVEF in untreated and iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice shown in Figure 4A-C.

claims.claim: The transcriptional response to intracellular iron deficiency in untreated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice was absent in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
claims.source: The transcriptional response to intracellular iron deficiency in untreated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice (upregulation of TfR1 mRNA and downregulation of Slc40a1 mRNA relative to Hampfl/fl controls), was absent in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, consistent with correction of cardiomyocyte iron deficiency (Figure 4D–E).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing TfR1 and Slc40a1 mRNA expression in untreated and iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice shown in Figure 4D-E.

claims.claim: Prevention of cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice by intravenous iron treatment confirms the causal relationship between cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and cardiac dysfunction.
claims.source: Prevention of cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice by intravenous iron treatment confirms the causal relationship between cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and cardiac dysfunction in this setting.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that iron supplementation prevented cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.

claims.claim: Aconitase I activity was significantly reduced in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 3 months and 6 months of age.
claims.source: We found that Aconitase I, Complex I and Complex IV activities were significantly reduced in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 3 months and 6 months of age, and that this reduction in activity was prevented in iron-treated 6-month old mice (Figure 4F–H).
claims.evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assays for Aconitase I in hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Complex I activity was significantly reduced in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 3 months and 6 months of age.
claims.source: We found that Aconitase I, Complex I and Complex IV activities were significantly reduced in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 3 months and 6 months of age, and that this reduction in activity was prevented in iron-treated 6-month old mice (Figure 4F–H).
claims.evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assays for Complex I in hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Complex IV activity was significantly reduced in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 3 months and 6 months of age.
claims.source: We found that Aconitase I, Complex I and Complex IV activities were significantly reduced in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 3 months and 6 months of age, and that this reduction in activity was prevented in iron-treated 6-month old mice (Figure 4F–H).
claims.evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assays for Complex IV in hearts of Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: The reduction in activity of Aconitase I, Complex I and Complex IV was prevented in iron-treated 6-month old Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
claims.source: We found that Aconitase I, Complex I and Complex IV activities were significantly reduced in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts compared to Hampfl/fl controls at 3 months and 6 months of age, and that this reduction in activity was prevented in iron-treated 6-month old mice (Figure 4F–H).
claims.evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assays in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice shown in Figure 4F-H.

claims.claim: Dilation of mitochondrial cristae was seen in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts as early as 3 months of age and progressed further at 6 months of age.
claims.source: By electron microscopy (EM), dilation of mitochondrial cristae was seen in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts as early as 3 months of age and progressed further at 6 months of age.
claims.evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images of hearts from Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice at 3 and 6 months shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial cristae dilation was prevented in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, which had healthy-looking mitochondria at 6 months of age.
claims.source: However, this was prevented in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, which had healthy-looking mitochondria at 6 months of age (Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images of hearts from iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: Expression of genes encoding Hexokinase 2 (Hk2), Enolase (Eno), and Lactate dehydrogenase A (Ldha) were all significantly increased at 3 months and 6 months of age in hearts of untreated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
claims.source: We found that expression of genes encoding Hexokinase 2 (Hk2) which catalyses the first step of glycolysis, Enolase (Eno), which catalyses the penultimate step of glycolysis and of Lactate dehydrogenase A (Ldha) which catalyses the ultimate step of glycolysis were all significantly increased at 3 months and 6 months of age in hearts of untreated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing Hk2, Eno, and Ldha mRNA expression in hearts of untreated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice versus controls shown in Figure 4J-L.

claims.claim: Upregulation of glycolytic genes was not seen in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.
claims.source: This upregulation of glycolytic genes was not seen in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice (Figure 4J–L).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data showing Hk2, Eno, and Ldha mRNA expression in iron-treated Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice shown in Figure 4J-L.

claims.claim: Reduction in the activities of key iron-containing metabolic enzymes, mitochondrial failure and upregulated glycolysis precede the development of cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that reduction in the activities of key iron-containing metabolic enzymes, mitochondrial failure and upregulated glycolysis precede the development of cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts, and are prevented by intravenous iron treatment.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the temporal sequence of observations showing metabolic changes at 3 months and cardiac dysfunction at 6 months in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.

claims.claim: Reduction in the activities of key iron-containing metabolic enzymes, mitochondrial failure and upregulated glycolysis are prevented by intravenous iron treatment in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that reduction in the activities of key iron-containing metabolic enzymes, mitochondrial failure and upregulated glycolysis precede the development of cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts, and are prevented by intravenous iron treatment.
claims.evidence: Supported by the combined observations that iron treatment prevented reductions in enzyme activities, mitochondrial abnormalities, and upregulation of glycolytic genes.

claims.claim: Cardiomyocyte hepcidin is required for autonomous cellular iron homeostasis.
claims.source: The major finding of this study is that cardiomyocyte hepcidin is required for autonomous cellular iron homeostasis.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that loss of cardiac hepcidin leads to cardiomyocyte iron deficiency despite normal systemic iron homeostasis.

claims.claim: Cardiac hepcidin operates in an autocrine fashion by regulating cardiomyocyte FPN.
claims.source: Loss of hepcidin responsiveness specifically in cardiomyocytes engendered the same effects as loss of cardiac hepcidin, demonstrating that cardiac hepcidin operates in an autocrine fashion by regulating cardiomyocyte FPN.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that both cardiac hepcidin deletion and cardiac FPN mutation resistant to hepcidin produce similar phenotypes.

claims.claim: A role in cellular iron homeostasis, and an autocrine mode of action for the HAMP/FPN axis have not been described previously in any other tissue.
claims.source: A role in cellular iron homeostasis, and an autocrine mode of action for the HAMP/FPN axis have not been described previously in any other tissue.
claims.evidence: Based on the authors' knowledge of the existing scientific literature on hepcidin and ferroportin function.

claims.claim: The cardiac HAMP/FPN axis is essential for normal heart function.
claims.source: A second important finding is that this cardiac HAMP/FPN axis is essential for normal heart function, and that its disruption leads to ultimately fatal cardiac metabolic and contractile dysfunction, even against a background of intact systemic iron homeostasis.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observations that disruption of the cardiac HAMP/FPN axis leads to cardiac dysfunction and increased mortality despite normal systemic iron indices.

claims.claim: Disruption of the cardiac HAMP/FPN axis leads to ultimately fatal cardiac metabolic and contractile dysfunction, even against a background of intact systemic iron homeostasis.
claims.source: A second important finding is that this cardiac HAMP/FPN axis is essential for normal heart function, and that its disruption leads to ultimately fatal cardiac metabolic and contractile dysfunction, even against a background of intact systemic iron homeostasis.
claims.evidence: Supported by the combined observations of increased mortality, cardiac dysfunction, and metabolic abnormalities in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice despite normal systemic iron indices.

claims.claim: Metabolic and contractile dysfunction are preceded by cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and prevented by intravenous iron supplementation.
claims.source: Metabolic and contractile dysfunction are preceded by cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and prevented by intravenous iron supplementation, indicating a causal relationship between cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and cardiac dysfunction.
claims.evidence: Supported by the temporal sequence of observations and the prevention of dysfunction by iron treatment.

claims.claim: There is a causal relationship between cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and cardiac dysfunction.
claims.source: Metabolic and contractile dysfunction are preceded by cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and prevented by intravenous iron supplementation, indicating a causal relationship between cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and cardiac dysfunction.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that iron supplementation prevents cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice.

claims.claim: Cardiomyocytes secrete an active HAMP peptide in a Furin-dependent manner.
claims.source: We found that Furin inhibition increased iron export from Hampfl/fl but not from Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ cardiomyocytes (Appendix 1—figure 1), demonstrating that cardiomyocytes secrete an active HAMP peptide in a Furin-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: Supported by Fe55 efflux experiments in cardiomyocytes treated with Furin inhibitor, referenced in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claims.claim: Differential regulation of Furin by iron may explain the divergent effects of iron on Hamp transcript and HAMP protein.
claims.source: These data suggest that differential regulation of Furin by iron may explain the divergent effects of iron on Hamp transcript and HAMP protein.
claims.evidence: Speculative inference based on the observed upregulation of Furin by iron deficiency and its role in HAMP secretion.

claims.claim: Upregulation of cardiac HAMP in mice fed an iron-deficient diet raises the possibility that it may be involved in protecting the heart in the setting of systemic iron deficiency.
claims.source: The upregulation of cardiac HAMP in mice fed an iron-deficient diet raises the possibility that it may be involved in protecting the heart in the setting of systemic iron deficiency.
claims.evidence: Speculative inference based on the observation that cardiac HAMP protein is increased by iron-deficient diet.

claims.claim: When provided an iron-deficient diet, Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice exhibited a greater cardiac hypertrophic response than their Hampfl/fl littermate controls.
claims.source: This hypothesis is supported by the finding that, when provided an iron-deficient diet, Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice exhibited a greater cardiac hypertrophic response than their Hampfl/fl littermate controls (Appendix 1—figure 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by data referenced in Appendix 1—figure 2 showing cardiac hypertrophic response in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice on iron-deficient diet.

claims.claim: Ubiquitous Hamp knockout and ubiquitous Slc40a1 C326Y knock-in mice do not develop the cardiac dysfunction seen in cardiomyocyte-specific Hamp knockout and cardiomyocyte-specific Slc40a1 C326Y knock-in mice.
claims.source: It is interesting that ubiquitous Hamp knockout (Lakhal-Littleton et al., 2015) and ubiquitous Slc40a1 C326Y knock-in mice (Appendix 1—figure 3), both models of systemic iron overload, do not develop the cardiac dysfunction seen in cardiomyocyte-specific Hamp knockout and cardiomyocyte-specific Slc40a1 C326Y knock-in mice.
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison with prior published data on ubiquitous Hamp knockout mice and data on ubiquitous Slc40a1 C326Y knock-in mice referenced in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claims.claim: Upregulation of cardiomyocyte FPN under conditions of normal iron availability is detrimental to cardiac function.
claims.source: This suggests that, while upregulation of cardiomyocyte FPN under conditions of normal iron availability (cardiac-specific models described in this study) is detrimental to cardiac function, it is protective under conditions of increased systemic iron availability (systemic models).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the comparison between cardiac-specific and systemic models of FPN upregulation.

claims.claim: Upregulation of cardiomyocyte FPN is protective under conditions of increased systemic iron availability.
claims.source: This suggests that, while upregulation of cardiomyocyte FPN under conditions of normal iron availability (cardiac-specific models described in this study) is detrimental to cardiac function, it is protective under conditions of increased systemic iron availability (systemic models).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that systemic models with iron overload do not develop cardiac dysfunction despite FPN upregulation.

claims.claim: Deletion of cardiomyocyte FPN resulted in fatal cardiomyocyte iron overload, preventable by dietary iron restriction.
claims.source: Previously, we also showed that deletion of cardiomyocyte FPN resulted in fatal cardiomyocyte iron overload, preventable by dietary iron restriction (Lakhal-Littleton et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by prior published work by the authors cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Iron levels within cardiomyocytes are a balance between cellular iron efflux which is regulated by the cardiac HAMP/FPN axis, and systemic iron availability which is regulated by the systemic HAMP/FPN axis.
claims.source: Together, our studies demonstrate that iron levels within cardiomyocytes are a balance between cellular iron efflux which is regulated by the cardiac HAMP/FPN axis, and systemic iron availability which is regulated by the systemic HAMP/FPN axis (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the combined observations across different mouse models showing the interplay between cardiac and systemic iron regulation, illustrated in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Iron overload is detrimental to cardiac health, as demonstrated by iron overload cardiomyopathy in hemochromatosis and thalassemia major patients.
claims.source: Iron overload is detrimental to cardiac health, as demonstrated by iron overload cardiomyopathy in hemochromatosis and thalassemia major patients (Gulati et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by prior published clinical studies on iron overload cardiomyopathy.

claims.claim: The cardiac HAMP/FPN axis may have a modifying effect on the severity of iron-overload cardiomyopathy.
claims.source: Our model of cardiac iron homeostasis implies that the cardiac HAMP/FPN axis may have a modifying effect on the severity of iron-overload cardiomyopathy.
claims.evidence: Speculative inference based on the proposed model of cardiac iron homeostasis.

claims.claim: There is a lack of concordance between the degrees of cardiac iron overload and liver iron overload in a significant proportion of hemochromatosis and thalassemia major patients.
claims.source: Thus, it would be interesting to explore whether differences in the levels of cardiac FPN and HAMP, possibly due to different local stimulatory and suppressive signals (e.g local inflammation, local ischemia), explain the reported lack of concordance between the degrees of cardiac iron overload and liver iron overload in a significant proportion of hemochromatosis and thalassemia major patients (Anderson et al., 2001; Noetzli et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by prior published clinical studies on iron overload in hemochromatosis and thalassemia patients.

claims.claim: Systemic iron deficiency correlates with functional and molecular markers of disease severity in patients with chronic heart failure (CHF).
claims.source: Indeed, systemic iron deficiency correlates with functional and molecular markers of disease severity in patients with chronic heart failure (CHF) (Klip et al., 2013; Comín-Colet et al., 2013),and also appears to contribute to the risk of death after an episode of acute heart failure (Jankowska et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by prior published clinical studies on iron deficiency in heart failure patients.

claims.claim: Iron deficiency appears to contribute to the risk of death after an episode of acute heart failure.
claims.source: Indeed, systemic iron deficiency correlates with functional and molecular markers of disease severity in patients with chronic heart failure (CHF) (Klip et al., 2013; Comín-Colet et al., 2013),and also appears to contribute to the risk of death after an episode of acute heart failure (Jankowska et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by prior published clinical studies on iron deficiency and mortality in heart failure patients.

claims.claim: The prevalence of iron deficiency in patients with CHF ranges between 30–50%.
claims.source: Given the high prevalence of iron deficiency in patients with CHF, ranging between 30–50% (Klip et al., 2013; Nanas et al., 2006; Ezekowitz et al., 2003), the European Society of Cardiology recently recommended the assessment of iron deficiency as a comorbidity in CHF.
claims.evidence: Supported by prior published clinical studies on the prevalence of iron deficiency in heart failure patients.

claims.claim: The European Society of Cardiology recently recommended the assessment of iron deficiency as a comorbidity in CHF.
claims.source: Given the high prevalence of iron deficiency in patients with CHF, ranging between 30–50% (Klip et al., 2013; Nanas et al., 2006; Ezekowitz et al., 2003), the European Society of Cardiology recently recommended the assessment of iron deficiency as a comorbidity in CHF.
claims.evidence: Based on established clinical guidelines from the European Society of Cardiology.

claims.claim: Several clinical trials have established the benefits of intravenous iron supplementation in CHF patients, with or without anaemia.
claims.source: Furthermore, several clinical trials have now established the benefits of intravenous iron supplementation in CHF patients, with or without anaemia (Ponikowski et al., 2015; Anker et al., 2009; Avni et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by prior published clinical trials on iron supplementation in heart failure patients.

claims.claim: The mechanisms underlying the anaemia-independent effects of iron deficiency and the benefits of intravenous iron in CHF patients are not fully understood.
claims.source: The mechanisms underlying the anaemia-independent effects of iron deficiency and the benefits of intravenous iron in CHF patients are not fully understood.
claims.evidence: Based on the authors' knowledge of the current state of understanding in the field.

claims.claim: Hamp mRNA and HAMP protein are elevated in the ischemic myocardium during the acute phase in the rat model of myocardial infarction (MI).
claims.source: It has been shown, in the rat model of myocardial infarction (MI), that Hamp mRNA and HAMP protein are elevated in the ischemic myocardium during the acute phase (Simonis et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by prior published studies in rat models of myocardial infarction.

claims.claim: Circulating HAMP was shown to be elevated in the serum within 4 hr of MI in humans.
claims.source: In humans, circulating HAMP was shown to be elevated in the serum within 4 hr of MI, although the tissue source of this hepcidin was not identified (Suzuki et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by prior published clinical studies on hepcidin levels in myocardial infarction patients.

claims.claim: Decreased cardiac HAMP expression has been reported in a transgenic mouse model of dilated cardiomyopathy.
claims.source: In addition, decreased cardiac HAMP expression has been reported in a transgenic mouse model of dilated cardiomyopathy, where the phenotype was ameliorated following transgenic overexpression of cardiac hepcidin (Zhang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by prior published studies in mouse models of dilated cardiomyopathy.

claims.claim: The phenotype of dilated cardiomyopathy in a transgenic mouse model was ameliorated following transgenic overexpression of cardiac hepcidin.
claims.source: In addition, decreased cardiac HAMP expression has been reported in a transgenic mouse model of dilated cardiomyopathy, where the phenotype was ameliorated following transgenic overexpression of cardiac hepcidin (Zhang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by prior published studies in mouse models of dilated cardiomyopathy.

claims.claim: Strategies that target the HAMP/FPN axis may impinge on cardiac iron homeostasis and function.
claims.source: Currently, there is considerable interest in targeting the HAMP/FPN axis for the treatment of iron overload and iron deficiency. Our studies suggest that such strategies may also impinge on cardiac iron homeostasis and function.
claims.evidence: Speculative inference based on the findings that cardiac HAMP/FPN axis is important for cardiac iron homeostasis and function.

claims.claim: Both FPN and hepcidin are found in the brain, kidney and placenta.
claims.source: Other than the heart, both FPN and hepcidin are also found in the brain, kidney and placenta (McCarthy and Kosman, 2014; Kulaksiz, 2005; Evans et al., 2011; Rouault, 2013; Moos and Rosengren Nielsen, 2006; Bastin et al., 2006; Wolff et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by prior published studies on FPN and hepcidin expression in various tissues.

claims.claim: Hepcidin is the master regulator of systemic iron homeostasis.
claims.source: Hepcidin is the master regulator of systemic iron homeostasis.
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific consensus on hepcidin's role in iron homeostasis.

claims.claim: Hepcidin is derived primarily from the liver.
claims.source: Derived primarily from the liver, it inhibits the iron exporter ferroportin in the gut and spleen, the sites of iron absorption and recycling respectively.
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific consensus on the primary source of hepcidin.

claims.claim: Hepcidin inhibits the iron exporter ferroportin in the gut and spleen, the sites of iron absorption and recycling respectively.
claims.source: Derived primarily from the liver, it inhibits the iron exporter ferroportin in the gut and spleen, the sites of iron absorption and recycling respectively.
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific consensus on hepcidin's mechanism of action.

claims.claim: Ferroportin is found in cardiomyocytes.
claims.source: Recently, we demonstrated that ferroportin is also found in cardiomyocytes, and that its cardiac-specific deletion leads to fatal cardiac iron overload.
claims.evidence: Supported by prior published work by the authors.

claims.claim: Cardiac-specific deletion of ferroportin leads to fatal cardiac iron overload.
claims.source: Recently, we demonstrated that ferroportin is also found in cardiomyocytes, and that its cardiac-specific deletion leads to fatal cardiac iron overload.
claims.evidence: Supported by prior published work by the authors.

claims.claim: Hepcidin is expressed in cardiomyocytes.
claims.source: Hepcidin is also expressed in cardiomyocytes, where its function remains unknown.
claims.evidence: Based on the authors' prior observations and established knowledge.

claims.claim: The function of hepcidin in cardiomyocytes remains unknown.
claims.source: Hepcidin is also expressed in cardiomyocytes, where its function remains unknown.
claims.evidence: Based on the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claims.claim: Both models (Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+) maintain normal systemic iron homeostasis.
claims.source: We find that while both models maintain normal systemic iron homeostasis, they nonetheless develop fatal contractile and metabolic dysfunction as a consequence of cardiomyocyte iron deficiency.
claims.evidence: Supported by measurements of systemic iron indices in both mouse models shown in Tables 1 and 3.

claims.claim: Both models (Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+) develop fatal contractile and metabolic dysfunction as a consequence of cardiomyocyte iron deficiency.
claims.source: We find that while both models maintain normal systemic iron homeostasis, they nonetheless develop fatal contractile and metabolic dysfunction as a consequence of cardiomyocyte iron deficiency.
claims.evidence: Supported by the combined observations of increased mortality, cardiac dysfunction, metabolic abnormalities, and cardiomyocyte iron deficiency in both mouse models.

claims.claim: These findings are the first demonstration of a cell-autonomous role for hepcidin in iron homeostasis.
claims.source: These findings are the first demonstration of a cell-autonomous role for hepcidin in iron homeostasis.
claims.evidence: Based on the authors' knowledge of the existing scientific literature.

claims.claim: The cell-autonomous function of hepcidin may also be important in other tissues that express both hepcidin and ferroportin, such as the kidney and the brain.
claims.source: They raise the possibility that such function may also be important in other tissues that express both hepcidin and ferroportin, such as the kidney and the brain.
claims.evidence: Speculative inference based on the findings in the heart and the known expression of hepcidin and ferroportin in other tissues.

claims.claim: Iron is essential for cellular functions as a constituent of hemoproteins, iron-sulphur proteins and other functional groups.
claims.source: As a constituent of hemoproteins, iron-sulphur proteins and other functional groups, iron is essential for cellular functions.
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about iron's role in cellular biochemistry.

claims.claim: Excess iron participates in cytotoxic Fenton-type chemical reactions.
claims.source: Conversely, excess iron participates in cytotoxic Fenton-type chemical reactions.
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about iron chemistry and toxicity.

claims.claim: Both iron deficiency and iron overload are detrimental to the cell.
claims.source: Thus, both iron deficiency and iron overload are detrimental to the cell.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the established knowledge that iron is essential but excess iron is toxic.

claims.claim: Cellular iron homeostasis is controlled by the Iron Regulatory Proteins IRPs.
claims.source: In mammals, cellular iron homeostasis is controlled by the Iron Regulatory Proteins IRPs.
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about cellular iron regulation.

claims.claim: Intracellular iron levels control the degradation of IRP2 and the conformational switch that confers the RNA-binding function of IRP1.
claims.source: Intracellular iron levels control the degradation of IRP2 and the conformational switch that confers the RNA-binding function of IRP1.
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about IRP regulation.

claims.claim: IRPs control the levels of iron uptake proteins such as transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) and divalent metal transporter (DMT1), and the iron storage protein ferritin.
claims.source: IRPs in turn control the levels of iron uptake proteins such as transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) and divalent metal transporter (DMT1), and the iron storage protein ferritin (Rouault and Klausner, 1997; Rouault, 2006).
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about IRP function, supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Systemic iron homeostasis is controlled by the hepcidin/ferroportin axis at the sites of iron entry into the circulation.
claims.source: Systemic iron homeostasis is controlled by the hepcidin/ferroportin axis at the sites of iron entry into the circulation.
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about systemic iron regulation.

claims.claim: Ferroportin (FPN) is the only known mammalian iron export protein.
claims.source: Ferroportin (FPN), which is encoded by the Solute Carrier Family 40 Member 1 (Slc40a1), is the only known mammalian iron export protein and mediates iron release into the circulation from duodenal enterocytes, splenic reticuloendothelial macrophages and hepatocytes, the sites of iron absorption, recycling and storage respectively (Ganz, 2005; Donovan et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about ferroportin, supported by cited references.

claims.claim: FPN mediates iron release into the circulation from duodenal enterocytes, splenic reticuloendothelial macrophages and hepatocytes.
claims.source: Ferroportin (FPN), which is encoded by the Solute Carrier Family 40 Member 1 (Slc40a1), is the only known mammalian iron export protein and mediates iron release into the circulation from duodenal enterocytes, splenic reticuloendothelial macrophages and hepatocytes, the sites of iron absorption, recycling and storage respectively (Ganz, 2005; Donovan et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about ferroportin function, supported by cited references.

claims.claim: FPN-mediated iron release is antagonized by the hormone hepcidin.
claims.source: FPN-mediated iron release is antagonized by the hormone hepcidin, also known as hepcidin antimicrobial peptide (HAMP).
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about hepcidin-ferroportin interaction.

claims.claim: Hepcidin is produced primarily in the liver.
claims.source: Produced primarily in the liver, hepcidin binds to and induces internalization of FPN, thereby limiting iron release into the circulation and its availability to peripheral tissues (Nemeth et al., 2004; Qiao et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about hepcidin production, supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Hepcidin binds to and induces internalization of FPN, thereby limiting iron release into the circulation and its availability to peripheral tissues.
claims.source: Produced primarily in the liver, hepcidin binds to and induces internalization of FPN, thereby limiting iron release into the circulation and its availability to peripheral tissues (Nemeth et al., 2004; Qiao et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about hepcidin mechanism of action, supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Hepcidin production is impaired in diseases of systemic iron overload such as hemochromatosis and β-thalassaemia.
claims.source: The importance of the HAMP/FPN axis is illustrated by diseases of systemic iron overload such as hemochromatosis and β-thalassaemia, where hepcidin production is impaired (Camaschella, 2005; Musallam et al., 2012), and in anaemia of chronic disease where hepcidin production is inappropriately elevated (De Falco et al., 2013; Nemeth and Ganz, 2014).
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about hepcidin dysregulation in disease, supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Hepcidin production is inappropriately elevated in anaemia of chronic disease.
claims.source: The importance of the HAMP/FPN axis is illustrated by diseases of systemic iron overload such as hemochromatosis and β-thalassaemia, where hepcidin production is impaired (Camaschella, 2005; Musallam et al., 2012), and in anaemia of chronic disease where hepcidin production is inappropriately elevated (De Falco et al., 2013; Nemeth and Ganz, 2014).
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about hepcidin dysregulation in disease, supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Hepcidin is found in tissues with no recognized role in systemic iron homeostasis, including the heart, the brain, the kidney and the placenta.
claims.source: Other than the liver, hepcidin is also found in tissues with no recognized role in systemic iron homeostasis, including the heart (Merle et al., 2007), the brain (McCarthy and Kosman, 2014), the kidney (Kulaksiz, 2005) and the placenta (Evans et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about extra-hepatic hepcidin expression, supported by cited references.

claims.claim: One hypothesis is that extra-hepatic hepcidin is involved in local iron control.
claims.source: The function of this extra-hepatic hepcidin remains unknown, but one hypothesis is that it is involved in local iron control.
claims.evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on the expression pattern of hepcidin.

results.result: Cardiac hepcidin expression is regulated by dietary iron at the mRNA level in both heart and liver, but cardiac HAMP protein responds differently than hepatic HAMP protein to iron manipulation. While hepatic HAMP protein changes mirror mRNA changes, cardiac HAMP protein increases with iron deficiency and is unaffected by iron loading.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 1A) and immunohistochemistry (Figure 1B) showing differential regulation of cardiac versus hepatic hepcidin at the protein level despite similar mRNA responses. The data demonstrate tissue-specific post-transcriptional regulation of hepcidin.

results.result: In primary cardiomyocytes, iron manipulation affects Hamp mRNA and HAMP protein secretion differently. FAC increases Hamp mRNA from 4 hours while DFO decreases it, but HAMP protein secretion is increased by DFO as early as 2 hours and unchanged by FAC.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 are supported by qPCR (Figure 1C) and ELISA (Figure 1D) data from primary cardiomyocytes. The divergent responses of mRNA and protein to iron manipulation are consistently demonstrated across multiple timepoints, confirming post-transcriptional regulation.

results.result: Furin mediates the increased secretion of active HAMP peptide from iron-deficient cardiomyocytes. Furin expression is upregulated by iron deficiency both in vivo and in vitro, and Furin inhibition prevents the DFO-induced increase in HAMP secretion.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13 and C68 are supported by qPCR data showing Furin upregulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), ELISA showing prevention of HAMP secretion by Furin inhibitor CMK (Figure 1D), and Fe55 efflux experiments (Appendix 1—figure 1). The mechanistic link between Furin and HAMP processing is well-established.

results.result: Cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of Hamp in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice results in near-complete ablation of cardiac hepcidin expression without affecting hepatic hepcidin, confirming cardiomyocytes as the primary source of cardiac hepcidin and the cardiac-specific nature of the deletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18 are supported by qPCR (Figure 1E) and immunohistochemistry (Figure 1F) showing dramatic reduction in cardiac but not hepatic hepcidin. The specificity of the Myh6.Cre system for cardiomyocytes is well-established, and the data confirm successful cardiac-specific knockout.

results.result: Cardiac-specific deletion of hepcidin does not affect systemic iron homeostasis. Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice maintain normal liver iron stores, circulating iron markers, and serum hepcidin levels compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C22 and C99 are supported by comprehensive measurements of systemic iron indices (Table 1) showing no differences between Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and control mice. This demonstrates that cardiac hepcidin functions locally rather than contributing to systemic iron regulation.

results.result: Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice develop fatal cardiac dysfunction characterized by increased mortality (71% by 52 weeks), left ventricular enlargement, cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, increased apoptosis, and reduced ejection fraction (from 62% to 42%) by 6 months of age.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C32 are supported by survival data (Figure 2A), histology (Figure 2B-G), and cine MRI measurements (Figure 2H-K). The phenotype is severe and progressive, with multiple independent measures confirming cardiac dysfunction. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=47-50 for survival, n=8-11 for MRI).

results.result: Both Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice show upregulated cardiac FPN and develop similar cardiac phenotypes including increased mortality, LV enlargement, cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, increased apoptosis, and reduced LVEF, demonstrating that loss of hepcidin responsiveness phenocopies loss of hepcidin.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C40 are supported by immunohistochemistry (Figure 3A-B), survival data (Figure 3C), histology (Figure 3D-I), and cine MRI (Figure 3J-L). The parallel phenotypes in both models strongly support the conclusion that cardiac hepcidin acts through FPN regulation. The C326Y mutation's specificity for hepcidin resistance is well-established in the literature.

results.result: Loss of cardiac hepcidin or hepcidin responsiveness results in upregulated FPN-mediated iron export, leading to cardiomyocyte iron deficiency. This is evidenced by increased Fe55 efflux, decreased cardiomyocyte iron content, and upregulation of iron deficiency markers (TfR1 upregulation, Slc40a1 downregulation).
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C47 are supported by Fe55 efflux assays (Figure 3M), ICP-MS measurements of cardiomyocyte iron (Figure 3N), and qPCR of iron regulatory genes (Figure 3O-P). The exogenous HAMP rescue experiment in C42 provides strong mechanistic evidence. The transcriptional responses are consistent with established iron deficiency signatures.

results.result: Intravenous iron supplementation prevents cardiac dysfunction in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice, corrects the transcriptional iron deficiency signature, and establishes a causal relationship between cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and cardiac dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50, C66-C67 are supported by cine MRI showing prevention of LV dysfunction (Figure 4A-C) and qPCR showing normalization of iron deficiency markers (Figure 4D-E) in iron-treated mice. This rescue experiment provides strong causal evidence. However, the iron treatment also affects systemic iron levels (Table 4), which could have indirect effects.

results.result: Cardiomyocyte iron deficiency in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice leads to reduced activity of iron-containing metabolic enzymes (Aconitase I, Complex I, Complex IV) and mitochondrial dysfunction (cristae dilation) at 3 and 6 months, which are prevented by iron supplementation.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C56 are supported by enzymatic activity assays (Figure 4F-H) and electron microscopy (Figure 4I). The temporal progression (3 months) precedes overt cardiac dysfunction (6 months), supporting a mechanistic sequence. Iron treatment rescues both enzyme activities and mitochondrial morphology, strengthening causality.

results.result: Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ hearts show upregulated glycolytic gene expression (Hk2, Eno, Ldha) at 3 and 6 months, which precedes cardiac dysfunction and is prevented by iron treatment, suggesting a metabolic shift from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 4J-L) showing increased glycolytic gene expression that is normalized by iron treatment. The temporal sequence (metabolic changes at 3 months, dysfunction at 6 months) supports the mechanistic interpretation. The glycolytic shift is consistent with mitochondrial dysfunction.

results.result: Cardiomyocyte hepcidin is required for autonomous cellular iron homeostasis and operates in an autocrine fashion by regulating cardiomyocyte FPN. This represents the first demonstration of a cell-autonomous role for hepcidin in iron homeostasis and is essential for normal cardiac function.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 and C101 represent the major conclusions of the study, supported by the combined evidence from both mouse models showing that cardiac-specific disruption of the HAMP/FPN axis causes cardiomyocyte iron deficiency and cardiac dysfunction despite normal systemic iron homeostasis. The novelty claim (C63, C101) regarding cell-autonomous function is reasonable based on the literature.

results.result: Differential regulation of Furin by iron may explain divergent effects on Hamp transcript versus HAMP protein, and cardiac HAMP upregulation during iron deficiency may protect the heart, as supported by greater cardiac hypertrophy in Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mice on iron-deficient diet.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are partially speculative. While C71 is supported by data (Appendix 1—figure 2), the mechanistic interpretation in C69 is speculative and would require additional experiments (e.g., Furin knockdown/overexpression studies). The protective role hypothesis (C70) is plausible but not definitively tested.

results.result: Cardiomyocyte iron content represents a balance between cardiac HAMP/FPN-regulated efflux and systemic HAMP/FPN-regulated iron availability. Upregulation of cardiomyocyte FPN is detrimental under normal iron availability but protective under systemic iron overload conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C76 are supported by comparison with prior published work (C75) and data on systemic models (C72, Appendix 1—figure 3). The model (Figure 5) integrates findings across multiple mouse models. However, the protective effect in systemic iron overload (C74) is inferred from absence of dysfunction rather than direct demonstration.

results.result: The cardiac HAMP/FPN axis may modify the severity of iron-overload cardiomyopathy in hemochromatosis and thalassemia patients, potentially explaining the reported lack of concordance between cardiac and liver iron overload in these conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 are speculative extensions to human disease. While C77 and C79 cite clinical literature, C78 is a hypothesis that would require clinical studies to test. The mouse data provide a plausible mechanistic basis but do not directly demonstrate this effect in human disease.

results.result: Iron deficiency is prevalent (30-50%) in chronic heart failure patients, correlates with disease severity and mortality, and benefits from intravenous iron supplementation, though the mechanisms underlying anaemia-independent effects are not fully understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C85 accurately summarize established clinical literature on iron deficiency in heart failure. These are background claims supported by cited clinical studies and guidelines. They provide context for the significance of the current findings but are not novel results of this study.

results.result: Cardiac hepcidin expression is altered in cardiac disease models and patients. Hepcidin is elevated in ischemic myocardium in rat MI models and in human serum after MI, while decreased cardiac hepcidin in a dilated cardiomyopathy mouse model is ameliorated by hepcidin overexpression.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 accurately cite prior published work on hepcidin in cardiac disease. These are background claims that provide context for the potential clinical relevance of the findings but are not novel results of this study.

results.result: Strategies targeting the HAMP/FPN axis for treating iron disorders may affect cardiac iron homeostasis and function. The cell-autonomous function of hepcidin may extend to other tissues expressing both hepcidin and ferroportin, such as brain, kidney, and placenta.
results.evaluation: Claims C90, C91, and C102 are speculative implications of the findings. While C91 cites literature on FPN/hepcidin expression in other tissues, the extension of cardiac findings to these tissues (C102) and the clinical implications (C90) are hypotheses requiring future investigation.

results.result: Background on iron biology and hepcidin/ferroportin system: Iron is essential but toxic in excess; cellular iron homeostasis is controlled by IRPs; systemic iron homeostasis is controlled by the liver-derived hormone hepcidin, which regulates ferroportin in gut, spleen, and liver. Extra-hepatic hepcidin exists but its function is unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C119 represent established background knowledge about iron biology and the hepcidin/ferroportin system, supported by cited literature and general scientific consensus. These provide necessary context but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Both Hampfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ and Slc40a1 C326Yfl/fl;Myh6.Cre+ mouse models develop fatal contractile and metabolic dysfunction as a consequence of cardiomyocyte iron deficiency despite maintaining normal systemic iron homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 is a summary conclusion supported by the combined evidence from both mouse models (Tables 1, 3; Figures 2-4). The dissociation between local cardiac and systemic iron homeostasis is a key finding demonstrated by multiple independent measures.
